A_target.statement:
Let $\alpha \in \R$ and $N \in \Z_{\ge 1}$.
Then there exist $p, q \in \Z$ with $1 \le q \le N$ and:
:$\size {q \alpha - p} < \dfrac 1 N$
In particular, if $\alpha$ is irrational then $\size {\alpha - \dfrac p q} < \dfrac 1 {q^2}$ for infinitely many fractions.

B_source.statement: If $n$ objects are placed in $m$ boxes with $n > m$, then some box contains at least two objects.

substitutions.the objects: the fractional parts of k alpha for k = 0, ..., N

derived.two objects in one box: a multiple q alpha within 1/N of an integer

object_map.reformulation: Place N + 1 fractional parts into N subintervals of [0, 1).

validity_conditions: Using N + 1 fractional parts and N boxes is exactly what the pigeonhole principle needs.
Infinitely many approximations for irrational alpha follow by letting N grow.
proof_plan: Consider the $N + 1$ fractional parts $\set {k \alpha}$ for $k = 0, 1, \ldots, N$, all in $\hointr 0 1$.
Divide $\hointr 0 1$ into the $N$ intervals $\hointr {\dfrac j N} {\dfrac {j + 1} N}$.
By the [[Pigeonhole Principle]], two of them, for $k < l$, lie in the same interval, so $\size {\set {l \alpha} - \set {k \alpha} } < \dfrac 1 N$.
